rounds.text: Rashi Peripherals Ltd is significantly under-appreciated by the market, trading at a modest P/E ratio of 16.4 [E1] despite phenomenal top-line and bottom-line compounding. Over recent trailing periods, sales have surged by 40% [E16] and profit growth has reached 50% [E19], heavily outstripping the sector median sales growth of 12.9% [E65] and sector median profit growth of 9.5% [E64]. Furthermore, a discounted cash flow valuation estimates intrinsic value at Rs 1724 per share compared to its current market price of Rs 786 [E39], offering a substantial margin of safety of 54.4% [E40]. A reverse DCF calculation reveals that the market price currently prices in a mere 5.2% earnings growth, a remarkably low bar against the 16.0% assumed in the base case [E41]. Underlying operational efficiency supports this strength, with a solid ROCE of 17.0% [E12] and rules-based screening awarding the stock a high-confidence BUY score of 93 out of 100 [E56]. Conceded: cash conversion stands at a weak 0.40x with operating cash flow trailing reported profit [E28], and institutional money flow currently registers as negative [E38].

The company exhibits a concerning disconnect between reported profits and actual cash generation, highlighted by a cash conversion ratio of just 0.40x for March 2026 as profits run far ahead of cash due to potential receivables or accruals [E28]. Furthermore, total borrowings have expanded to Rs 991 Cr in March 2026 from Rs 910 Cr a year earlier, adding leverage pressure [E33]. Institutional behavior reflects caution, with domestic institutions cutting their stake from 14.41% in March 2024 to 11.89% by September 2026 [E37], resulting in negative money flow and institutional outflow signals [E38, E61]. Valuation and pricing dynamics also flash warning signs, as recent price growth has outpaced profit growth by 88%, showing expectations running far ahead of delivery [E51], alongside a higher EV/EBITDA of 11.16x compared to the sector benchmark of 10.83x [E11]. Conceded: [E14], [E16], [E19], [E39], [E56].

Conceded: [E28], [E33], and [E61]. Despite the bear's focus on cash conversion and rising borrowings, operating cash flow reached Rs 114 Cr and free cash flow hit Rs 106 Cr in March 2026, proving the business generates substantial actual liquidity [E29, E30]. While domestic institutions reduced their holdings, foreign institutions actively increased their stake from 1.63% to 3.99% between March 2024 and September 2026 [E36]. The EV/EBITDA multiple of 11.16x is largely offset by a modest overall P/E of 16.4x to 17.12x, which remains below the sector benchmark of 19.58x [E1, E6, E11]. Most importantly, the reverse DCF demonstrates that the current market price implies a meager 5.2% earnings growth, drastically under-appreciating the company's proven 50% TTM profit growth and rules-based score of 93 out of 100 [E19, E41, E56].

Conceded: [E29, E30]. However, pointing to absolute operating and free cash flow figures ignores the glaring warning of a 0.40x cash conversion ratio for March 2026, which demonstrates that reported profits are running far ahead of actual cash collection and points directly to mounting receivables or accruals [E28]. Furthermore, while FII stakes rose over a multi-year period, domestic institutions have drawn down their holdings from 14.41% to 11.89%, contributing to a current signal of negative institutional money flow and recent quarterly promoter trimming of 0.49% [E37, E38, E54]. The argument that valuation is universally cheap is undercut by an EV/EBITDA multiple of 11.16x that actually trades at a premium to the sector benchmark of 10.83x, alongside a price-to-book ratio of 2.75x that also exceeds its sector benchmark [E7, E11]. Finally, relying on TTM profit growth of 50% [E19] and a high rules-based score [E56] dismisses the reality that price growth recently outpaced profit growth by 88% and that operating margins remain stuck at a flat 3% with an inconsistent trend [E26, E51].

Conceded: [E28, E54]. The bear's concern over cash conversion is more than offset by actual positive generation of Rs 114 Cr in operating cash flow and Rs 106 Cr in free cash flow for March 2026 [E29, E30]. While domestic institutions trimmed their stake [E37], foreign institutions have steadily accumulated shares from 1.63% to 3.99% [E36], and overall promoter holding sits higher at 63.55% compared to 63.41% in March 2024 [E35]. The slight EV/EBITDA and P/B sector premiums [E7, E11] are completely justified given that the company delivers superior ROCE of 15.84% against the sector benchmark of 11.93% [E10], alongside robust TTM sales and profit growth of 40% and 50% [E16, E19] that easily outpace sector medians [E64, E65]. Finally, the flat operating margin of 3% [E24] has proven perfectly adequate to power a massive acceleration in earnings, backed by a top-tier rules-based screen score of 93 out of 100 [E56].

Conceded: [E29, E30]. Despite positive absolute cash generation, the low cash conversion of 0.40x for March 2026 demonstrates that reported profits are running far ahead of actual cash collected, pointing directly to risks in receivables and accruals [E28]. While foreign institutions increased their holdings, domestic institutions reduced their stake from 14.41% to 11.89% [E37], resulting in negative institutional money flow and overall institutional outflow signals [E38, E61]. Furthermore, the recent promoter holding decrease of 0.49% directly contradicts long-term stability claims [E54]. The bull's reliance on backward-looking growth figures ignores that price growth recently exceeded profit growth by 88%, showing that expectations are running dangerously ahead of actual delivery in a business where operating margins remain stubbornly stuck at an inconsistent 3% [E24, E26, E51].
